name: Alternative Metal
about: Alternative metal took shape in the late 1980s when American bands raised on hardcore, funk, post-punk and noise rock started borrowing metal's weight without its rules. Faith No More, Jane's Addiction and Living Colour set it in motion; Soundgarden, Helmet and Primus pushed the rhythms into odd meters and drop-tuned sludge; Rage Against the Machine fused riffs with rap, and Tool turned the form into long-form art rock. Mike Patton's shape-shifting voice and Maynard James Keenan's controlled menace remain its two defining instruments. In the late 1990s Deftones and System of a Down carried it into the nu metal era while keeping their credibility, and today the lineage runs through bands like Chevelle, Loathe and Spiritbox, where heaviness and texture matter more than speed.

artists.name: Faith No More
artists.why: Mike Patton's band, the style's architects

artists.name: Soundgarden
artists.why: Sabbath weight, odd meters, Cornell's voice

artists.name: Tool
artists.why: turned the form into long-form art rock

artists.name: System of a Down
artists.why: Armenian folk, thrash and political satire

albums.title: Nothing's Shocking
albums.why: Perry Farrell's decadent howl and Dave Navarro's Zeppelin-sized guitars made the record that proved metal could be art-school music.

albums.title: Vivid
albums.why: Vernon Reid's band blew funk, jazz and Hendrix through hard rock on Cult of Personality and shamed the genre's segregation.

albums.title: The Real Thing
albums.why: Mike Patton's arrival turned a cult band into a hit with Epic, and the record's keyboards, funk and thrash sketched the whole genre.

albums.title: Louder Than Love
albums.why: The major-label debut is heavier and sludgier than anything that followed, a Sabbath-worshipping bridge between SST and Badmotorfinger.

albums.title: Ritual de lo Habitual
albums.why: Half hit singles and half sprawling, ecstatic epics, the second album closed the band's first life with Three Days as its monument.

albums.title: Facelift
albums.why: Before the grunge boom, Layne Staley and Jerry Cantrell's harmonies and Man in the Box made the first Seattle record to go platinum.

albums.title: Sailing the Seas of Cheese
albums.why: Les Claypool's rubbery bass led Jerry Was a Race Car Driver and Tommy the Cat into a weird, funny and genuinely heavy major-label debut.

albums.title: Badmotorfinger
albums.why: Rusty Cage, Outshined and Jesus Christ Pose in odd meters and alternate tunings, with Chris Cornell at full strength: the band's heaviest great record.

albums.title: Angel Dust
albums.why: Patton and the band buried a hit act under samples, easy listening, death metal and Midlife Crisis, and it has only grown in stature since.

albums.title: Meantime
albums.why: Page Hamilton's clipped, drop-D riffs and John Stanier's drumming on Unsung became the rhythmic template for a decade of heavy music.

albums.title: Rage Against the Machine
albums.why: Zack de la Rocha's rap polemics over Tom Morello's turntable-like guitar made a debut that still sounds like nothing else and sold millions.

albums.title: Undertow
albums.why: Sober and Prison Sex introduced Maynard James Keenan's controlled menace and Adam Jones's patient riffs before the band's ambitions outgrew the format.

albums.title: Houdini
albums.why: Partly produced by Kurt Cobain, Buzz Osborne's major-label debut is the slow, heavy, deadpan source that sludge and stoner bands keep drawing on.

albums.title: Betty
albums.why: Looser and stranger than Meantime, with jazz and blues detours around Milquetoast and Wilma's Rainbow, it confused fans and aged well.

albums.title: Astro-Creep: 2000
albums.why: Rob Zombie's B-movie samples and groove-metal riffs reached their commercial peak on More Human than Human, a loud cartoon done well.

albums.title: Ænima
albums.why: Justin Chancellor's arrival and Stinkfist, Forty Six & 2 and the title track made a dense, misanthropic record that remains the genre's artistic peak.

albums.title: Evil Empire
albums.why: Bulls on Parade led a harder, funkier second album that proved the debut's formula had more in it than one explosion.

albums.title: Around the Fur
albums.why: My Own Summer (Shove It) and Be Quiet and Drive showed Chino Moreno's whisper-to-scream range and the band's first real sense of atmosphere.

albums.title: System of a Down
albums.why: Serj Tankian's operatic rant and Daron Malakian's Armenian-inflected riffs made Sugar and Suite-Pee a debut unlike anything else in nu metal's orbit.

albums.title: White Pony
albums.why: Change (In the House of Flies) and Digital Bath wrapped shoegaze and trip-hop around heavy guitars, the record that split Deftones from their peers for good.

albums.title: Toxicity
albums.why: Chop Suey!, Aerials and the title track made a chart-topping record of thrash, folk melody and political satire that holds up as the band's best.

albums.title: Wonder What's Next
albums.why: The Loeffler brothers' Tool-indebted riffs and The Red made a tight, melodic record that kept alternative metal on the radio through the 2000s.

albums.title: I Let It In and It Took Everything
albums.why: The Liverpool band's Deftones-schooled mix of shoegaze haze and djent crunch gave the genre its most talked-about new record in years.

albums.title: Eternal Blue
albums.why: Courtney LaPlante's clean-and-scream range over Mike Stringer's riffs on Circle with Me and Holy Roller made a polished debut that broke the band wide.
